scenes.title: A busy recruitment week
scenes.description: Amina works in HR. Her calendar fills with interviews for a new office administrator. Her laptop shows a company-approved AI assistant.
lines: Meet Amina.
She works in HR at a growing company, and this is a busy week.
Her team is hiring a new office administrator, and Amina is preparing the interview materials.
There’s a lot to do, so she decides to try the AI assistant her company has approved for staff.
It could save her time.
But as she’s about to find out, knowing when to check AI’s work matters just as much as knowing how to use it.

scenes.title: A useful starting point
scenes.description: Amina gives the assistant the public job description and asks for interview questions and a job summary. A list and a summary type out within seconds.
lines: Amina gives the assistant the public job description and asks: “Suggest ten interview questions for this role, and write a short summary of the job for candidates.”
Within seconds, she has a list and a summary.
That’s genuinely helpful.
Instead of a blank page, she has a first draft to review and improve.
This is generative AI at work: creating new text from her request.

scenes.title: Something isn't right
scenes.description: The summary claims a driving licence is required, which the job description never mentions. A question about children is struck out as unrelated and unfair. Amina checks the approved interview guidance.
lines: But as Amina reads, two things catch her eye.
The summary says the role requires a driving licence.
The job description never mentions one.
The assistant made it up, and it sounded completely confident.
Then there’s question seven: “Do you have children, or are you planning to?”
That has nothing to do with the job, and asking it could treat candidates unfairly.
Amina removes the question, corrects the summary and checks everything against the company’s approved interview guidance.

scenes.title: Protecting people's information
scenes.description: A colleague suggests pasting applicants' CVs into an AI website. A privacy checklist appears and Amina closes the window.
lines: Later, a colleague has an idea.
“Why don’t we paste all the applicants’ CVs into an AI website and ask it to pick the best ones?”
Amina stops.
Those CVs contain names, addresses and work histories.
They belong to real people who shared them for one purpose.
Before putting personal information into any tool, she needs to know it’s approved, secure and allowed under her company’s privacy rules.
Just because a tool can process information doesn’t mean it’s the right place for it.

scenes.title: Who makes the decision?
scenes.description: An interview panel assesses candidates against the same agreed criteria. The AI assistant is set aside, and the panel is responsible for the decision.
lines: And who should choose the new administrator?
Not the AI.
The assistant helped Amina prepare, but it doesn’t know the candidates, and it can repeat unfair patterns from the information it learned from.
The interview panel assesses every candidate against the same agreed criteria, and the panel is responsible for the decision.
When a choice affects someone’s job, people need to stay in charge.

scenes.title: Stay in charge
scenes.description: Four question cards, correct, fair, private and who decides, tick off over Amina's finished materials.
lines: By the end of the week, Amina has a clear way of working with AI.
Before she uses anything it produces, she asks four questions.
Is it correct?
Is it fair?
Am I protecting people’s information?
And is this a decision a person should make?
AI can help us write, organise ideas and save time.
But it can also make mistakes, sound sure when it’s wrong and miss what matters.
So let it help with the work, and keep people responsible for the decisions.
That’s the end of Module 1’s lessons.
Well done.
